This example appears to imply that coordination will always dominate noncoordination. It is important to recall that the only source of disturbance was a common aggregate supply shock. The case of asymmetric shocks is addressed in problem 4 at the end of this chapter. But even when there are only common shocks, coordination need not always be superior. Rogo¤ (1985a) provided a counterexample. His argument is based on a model in which optimal policy is time-inconsistent (see chapter 7) but one can briefly describe the intuition behind Rogo¤’s results. A coordinated monetary expansion leads to a larger short-run real output expansion because it avoids changes in the real exchange rate. But this fact increases the incentive to engineer a surprise monetary expansion if the policymakers believe the natural rate of output is too low. Wage and price setters will anticipate this tactic, together with the associated higher inflation. Equilibrium involves higher inflation, but because it has been anticipated, output (which depends on inflation surprises) does not increase. Consequently, coordination leads to better stabilization but higher average inflation. If the costs of the latter are high enough, noncoordination can dominate coordination.
